concept.name: Collar
concept.definition: A collar is a position long the underlying asset, long an out-of-the-money put (the floor), and short an out-of-the-money call (the cap) on the same underlying and expiration; the call premium finances part or all of the put. It brackets the position's value between the two strikes.
concept.intuition: You give up the big upside above the call strike to pay for protection against the big downside below the put strike — outcome is 'collared' into a band.
concept.mechanics: Hold 100 shares, buy a put at K1 below the price, sell a call at K2 above it. A 'zero-cost collar' chooses strikes so the call premium equals the put premium. Value at expiration is bounded between K1 and K2 (plus net premium effects).
concept.formula: Value at expiration per share = min(max(S_T, K1), K2) plus/minus net premium; K1 = put strike (floor), K2 = call strike (cap).
concept.failure_modes: The short cap creates regret and assignment risk in strong rallies, and the floor still leaves the band between strikes exposed. Zero-cost construction often forces an uncomfortably tight cap or a distant floor.
concept.misconceptions: A collar is not a free hedge: the put is paid for by surrendered upside, which is a real economic cost. Nor does a zero-cost collar lock in current value — it only bounds the range of outcomes.
concept.example: Own XYZ at $100; buy the $90 put for $2 and sell the $110 call for $2 (zero cost). At expiration the position is worth between $90 and $110 per share no matter where XYZ trades.
